item.title: AWS Sign-In Adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization for AI Agents via ID-JAG
item.description:
AWS Sign-In Adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization for AI Agents via ID-JAG

AWS Sign‑In is adding Enterprise‑Managed Authorization (EMA) that lets organizations authorize AI agents such as Claude to access AWS MCP Server using existing enterprise identity providers like Okta.

🔍 Overview

  • EMA extends the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to let enterprises centrally control AI‑application access to protected resources.
  • It uses the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID‑JAG), an OAuth‑based grant that works with enterprise IdPs.

🧩 How it works

  1. Employee authentication – The employee signs in to an AI application (e.g., Claude) through single sign‑on (SSO) with an enterprise IdP such as Okta.
  2. ID‑JAG request – When the AI application needs to call an AWS MCP Server, it asks the IdP for an ID‑JAG assertion for the target resource.
  3. Enterprise authorization – The IdP evaluates policies defined by administrators and, if authorized, issues a short‑lived, signed ID‑JAG assertion.
  4. Token exchange with AWS Sign‑In – The AI application sends the ID‑JAG to the AWS Sign‑In OAuth token endpoint. AWS validates the assertion, checks the associated IAM role trust policy via AWS STS, and issues an OAuth access token linked to that role.
  5. Access AWS MCP Server – The AI application presents the OAuth token to the AWS MCP Server. The server validates the token, and the IAM role’s policies determine which AWS operations the agent may perform.

⚙️ Key details

  • No extra credentials – Employees do not need to manage long‑term AWS credentials or complete separate consent flows.
  • Policy‑driven – Administrators define access rules in the IdP, eliminating per‑user authorizations for each MCP server.
  • IAM enforcement – After token issuance, standard IAM role permissions control the actions the AI agent can perform on AWS resources.
  • Short‑lived assertions – ID‑JAG tokens are short‑lived and signed, limiting exposure if compromised.

🛠️ Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permission to configure IAM identity providers, roles, and policies.
  • An Okta organization with administrative rights to manage applications and Cross‑App Access policies.
  • An AI application (e.g., Claude) that supports EMA and ID‑JAG.
  • Access to an AWS MCP Server that supports OAuth‑based Enterprise‑Managed Authorization.
  • The AWS Region where the integration will be configured.

#AWS #AIAgents #EnterpriseAuthorization #Okta #OAuth

Source: Secure agentic access to AWS with Enterprise-Managed Authorization | Amazon Web Services

item.title: New Extortion Group Inception Targets SSO Credentials; ShinyHunters Claims Return
item.description:
New Extortion Group Inception Targets SSO Credentials; ShinyHunters Claims Return

🕵️ Inception Targets Global Brands

A newly formed data extortion group named ‘Inception’ has been linked to a large-scale campaign targeting single sign-on (SSO) credentials of multiple global brands. The gang surfaced on November 17, claiming seven victims on its extortion site, including chip maker AMD, PepsiCo, Cigna Healthcare, AutoZone, and Lucid Motors. However, none of these companies have publicly confirmed a data breach.

Cybersecurity company ReversingLabs has tracked the group’s activity since late October, identifying an extensive infrastructure that includes 21 domains used for SSO phishing, 41 domains believed to be part of the campaign infrastructure, and 4 other domains with suspected use. This infrastructure impersonates dozens of major corporations, including Dropbox, Duolingo, Western Union, Indeed, Activision Blizzard, Riot Games, Twitch, Reddit, Nestlé, Anthropic, Nintendo, Starbucks, McDonald’s, Paramount, and NBCUniversal. The existence of these domains does not prove those firms have been breached or targeted yet.

⚙️ Tactics and Infrastructure

The Inception campaign appears to rely on phone-based social engineering rather than email phishing, strongly resembling tactics used by the ShinyHunters extortion group. The actors use legal-themed websites that imitate corporate authentication services, primarily Okta but also NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager.

Component Details
Phishing Domains 21 domains identified by ReversingLabs
Infrastructure Domains 41 domains believed to be used in the campaign
Suspected Domains 4 additional domains with suspected use
Impersonated Brands Includes Dropbox, Duolingo, Western Union, and Nintendo
Authentication Services Okta, NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager

Okta published a report linking Inception to threat cluster O-UNC-053, which was previously associated with ShinyHunters and active since March. According to Okta, after law enforcement disrupted ShinyHunters, O-UNC-053 continued to register new phishing domains. In late October, the cluster launched a legal-themed campaign, and in mid-November, the Inception leak site went live. Okta assessed that the cluster very likely changed its brand affiliation, maintaining consistent infrastructure and TTPs.

Inception responded to these links by claiming on its extortion page that it operates independently and has no affiliation to previous groups. The actors argued that overlapping targets and common domain registration services do not establish operational links, noting that private tooling circulates among independent threat actors.

📢 ShinyHunters Reemerges

Following a series of arrests targeting alleged ShinyHunters members, the group claimed to have returned on November 23 via a new Tor site. The site contains messages in Russian and English announcing the group’s return and distancing itself from alleged impostors. The operators denounced a former member, reportedly arrested and cooperating with law enforcement, and mocked other individuals tied to the investigation, including Umbreon and Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky.

To verify their identity, the new operators published two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys dating back to 2020. BleepingComputer confirmed that both messages were signed using known PGP keys associated with the group, indicating access to the private signing keys. However, these keys do not confirm that the individuals behind the new operation are the same people who previously controlled the group, as the keys have circulated among numerous people. The operators stated they plan to launch a new CDN for hosting stolen data and will communicate exclusively through a specific Exploit hacking forum account and the new Tor site.

🛡️ Defending Against the Threat

ReversingLabs recommends enforcing phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, and strengthening help desk identity verification procedures to defend against the Inception campaign. Security teams should carefully review DNS, proxy, and identity provider logs dating back to October 21, 2026, for signs of suspicious activity.

#ShinyHunters #Inception #SSO #DataExtortion #Phishing #Okta

Source: New Inception extortion gang launches large-scale vishing campaign Source: ShinyHunters claims to return after FBI arrests, uses old PGP keys as proof

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds EKS‑run agent with Okta‑driven governance
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds EKS‑run agent with Okta‑driven governance

A second coding agent was added on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and wired through the same Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The update shows that the gateway‑based front door works regardless of where an agent runs, while keeping the Okta‑driven delegation and Cedar policy enforcement intact.

🔍 Overview

  • The original agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime and is invoked for signed‑in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA).
  • Okta decides which agent may act for a user and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity redeems Okta’s grant inside the agent.
  • The new addition is a second agent (agent B) deployed on Amazon EKS, using its own Okta identity but following the identical request flow.

🏗️ Architecture

  • All agents reach a single Gateway endpoint; the Gateway holds the target registry and redeems the Okta grant.
  • The topology consists of:
    • 1 agent (original) + 1 agent (EKS)
    • 2 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers acting as Gateway targets
    • Authorization checks embedded in each MCP server
  • Request flow (illustrated for agent A):
    1. User signs in; the backend‑for‑frontend (BFF) exchanges the ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID‑JAG).
    2. BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID‑JAG.
    3. Agent forwards the ID‑JAG to the Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session.
    4. Gateway inbound authorizer (issuer: Okta org auth server, audience: custom auth server, allowedClients pinned to the agent) accepts only that ID‑JAG.
    5. Cedar policies are evaluated for each tool listing and call before the Gateway invokes a target.
    6. For permitted calls, the Gateway uses AgentCore Identity to redeem the ID‑JAG for the target at Okta’s custom authorization server via the credential provider.
    7. Each hop emits OpenTelemetry spans collected by AgentCore Observability and visible in Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search.
    8. Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge.
  • Agent B on EKS follows the identical path through its own Gateway instance.
Component Role
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime Executes each task in an isolated session inside the AWS account
Okta Cross App Access (XAA) Determines which agent may act for a signed‑in user
AgentCore Identity Redeems Okta’s grant inside the agent and at the Gateway
Gateway Single front door; holds target registry, redeems grants, enforces Cedar policies
MCP servers Act as Gateway targets; perform outbound token‑exchange via credential provider
Cedar policy set Default‑deny policies evaluated at the Gateway before tools run
AgentCore Observability (CloudWatch) Central view of all decisions and OpenTelemetry spans
BFF Exchanges user ID token for ID‑JAG and starts the agent session

🔐 Security & Governance

  • Governance is proven by a deliberately small topology and a default‑deny Cedar policy set evaluated at the Gateway.
  • The agent’s role holds no token‑exchange or secret permissions; all authorizations are performed by the Gateway.
  • Policies bind each tool to the specific agent and the scope delegated by Okta.
  • The inbound authorizer mirrors the runtime authorizer from the original deployment.
  • Each MCP server has a static tool schema (listingMode = DEFAULT) so Cedar policies reference fixed tool names.

📈 Observability & Auditing

  • AgentCore Observability (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore) streams every decision to Amazon CloudWatch.
  • OpenTelemetry spans from each hop are indexed by CloudWatch Transaction Search.
  • Okta’s System Log is forwarded to CloudWatch via Amazon EventBridge, providing a complete audit trail.

💰 Cost & Deployment

  • Adding the second agent and the associated Gateway logic took about 90 minutes.
  • Amazon EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus node and Auto‑Mode management fees; AgentCore features are billed based on usage.
  • The solution builds on the AWS sample 08‑okta‑xaa‑delegation‑chain on GitHub, with Part 2 additions layered on top.

✅ When to use

Good fit

  • Scoped feature work, bug fixes, and tests on a trusted repository that declares its own setup and test commands.

Not a fit

  • Untrusted code, because the agent runs the repository’s own commands without additional safety checks.
  • Open‑ended work, because each task stops after three attempts.

The update demonstrates that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can securely orchestrate remote coding agents from multiple runtimes, while preserving strict Okta‑driven access control, Cedar‑based tool gating, and end‑to‑end observability.

#AWS #Bedrock #AIagents #Okta #Security

Source: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2 | Amazon Web Services Source: Extend Claude Code to remote sessions on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with security controls | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Integrates with Okta Cross App Access for Secure Agent Governance
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Integrates with Okta Cross App Access for Secure Agent Governance

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale using any framework or model. A new integration with Okta Cross App Access (XAA) allows organizations to manage agent identity and governance directly within their identity provider (IdP).

🔍 Overview

This solution establishes a clear separation between governance and execution. Okta serves as the governance plane, deciding which agent may act for which user against specific resources. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore serves as the execution plane, managing credentials and turning governance decisions into valid access tokens.

Component Role
Okta Governance plane: decides which agent acts for which user against which resource.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity Execution plane: holds credentials and redeems grants for tokens in a vault.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime Validates Okta’s grant.

🧩 How it works

The identity flow ensures that agent actions are always tied to a verified user session:

  • User Sign-in: Users access a backend for frontend (BFF) using OpenID Connect via the agent’s linked Okta app.
  • Token Exchange: For each request, the BFF performs an RFC 8693 token exchange, trading the user’s ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) at Okta’s authorization server.
  • Okta Verification: Okta checks that the agent is active, the user is assigned to it, and an administrator has approved the applications and scopes the agent might reach.
  • Execution: The BFF invokes the agent on the AgentCore runtime using the ID-JAG. AgentCore Identity then redeems the ID-JAG for a short-lived access token accepted by the resource.

⚙️ Key details

The system utilizes three distinct tokens to record different decisions throughout the request lifecycle:

  • ID Token: Identifies the user.
  • Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG): Represents Okta’s decision; single-use and expires in 5 minutes.
  • Access Token: Issued by Okta’s custom authorization server, naming both the user and the agent.

In testing, the governance process proved highly responsive. When an administrator removed a user’s assignment, Okta refused new agent requests for that user within approximately 1 second. Existing tokens expired within 5 minutes. Performance testing showed that AgentCore Identity added roughly 0.6 seconds of latency to a request taking 30 seconds end to end.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore charges based on usage. A technical walkthrough for building a task agent with this governance model takes about 1 hour. The associated sample code is provided for non-production use, and organizations should consult with security and legal teams before deployment.

#AWS #AmazonBedrock #Okta #AIagents #Cybersecurity

Source: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1 | Amazon Web Services
